modern: We mustn’t expect to see an immediate reward for all the good we do, and we mustn’t always limit our efforts to places and people that look likely to repay us for our work. The Egyptian throws his seed onto the waters of the Nile, where it might look like a sheer waste of grain. But in due time the flood goes down, the rice or other grain sinks into the fertile mud, and a harvest quickly springs up. Today let’s do good to the ungrateful and the evil. Let’s teach the careless and the stubborn. Unlikely waters may cover hopeful soil. Nowhere will our work be in vain in the Lord.

Our part is to cast our bread upon the waters; it is up to God to keep the promise, “Thou shalt find it.” He won’t let his promise fail. The good word we have spoken will live, will be found, and will be found by us. Maybe not just yet, but some day we will reap what we have sown. We must use our patience, for perhaps the Lord will put it to the test. “After many days,” says Scripture, and in many cases those days run into months and years, and yet the Word stands true. God’s promise will keep; let’s make sure we keep the command, and keep it today.

notes.note: Repayment; reward.
In British English, any grain, not only maize.
“For he is kind unto the unthankful and to the evil” ([[Luke.6.35|Luke 6:35]]).
Stubborn.

notes.term: Our labor shall not be in vain in the Lord
notes.note: “Your labour is not in vain in the Lord” ([[1Cor.15.58|1 Corinthians 15:58]]).

notes.term: We must exercise our patience; for perhaps the Lord may exercise it
notes.note: A play on words: we must put our patience to work, because the Lord may put it to the test.
A command.

modern: The Assyrian was allowed to oppress the Lord’s people for a time, but the time came for his power to be broken. In the same way, many a heart is held in slavery by Satan and chafes painfully under the yoke. Oh, that to such prisoners of hope the word of the Lord would come at once, as in the text: “Now will I break his yoke from off thee, and will burst thy bonds in sunder”!

Look! The Lord promises deliverance now: “Now will I break his yoke from off thee.” Believe for immediate freedom, and as your faith is, so it will be done for you this very hour. When God says “now,” let no one say “tomorrow.”

See how complete the rescue is to be: the yoke isn’t to be taken off but broken, and the bonds aren’t to be untied but burst apart. Here is a display of divine force that guarantees the oppressor won’t come back. His yoke is broken; we can’t be bowed down by its weight again. His bonds are burst apart; they can’t hold us any more. Oh, to believe in Jesus for complete and everlasting freedom! “If the Son shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed.” Come, Lord, and set your captives free, as you have promised.

notes.note: Chafes painfully; struggles against it.
“Turn you to the strong hold, ye prisoners of hope” ([[Zech.9.12|Zechariah 9:12]]).
Apart; in pieces. “Asunder” means the same.

notes.term: According to thy faith so shall it be unto thee
notes.note: Jesus to the two blind men: “According to your faith be it unto you” ([[Matt.9.29|Matthew 9:29]]).
Being set free, especially from slavery.

notes.term: If the Son shall make you free
notes.note: [[John.8.36|John 8:36]]. The King James reads “If the Son therefore shall make you free.”

modern: This confidence of the man of God amounts to a promise, for whatever faith is persuaded of is God’s purpose. The prophet had to cross the deep places of poverty and famine, but he went downhill without slipping, for the Lord gave him firm footing. Before long he was called up to the high places on the hills of conflict, and he was no more afraid to go up than to go down.
Look! The Lord lent him strength. No—Jehovah himself was his strength. Think of that: Almighty God himself becomes our strength!

Notice that the Lord also made him sure-footed. Deer leap over rock and crag and never miss their footing. Our Lord will give us grace to follow the hardest paths of duty without a stumble. He can fit our feet for the crags, so that we will be at home where, without God, we would perish.

One of these days we will be called to higher places still. Up there we will climb, to the mount of God, the high places where the shining ones are gathered. Oh, what feet the feet of faith are, by which, following the Hind of the Morning, we will go up into the hill of the Lord!

notes.note: A hind is a female deer, famously sure-footed on steep rock.
Equal to; amounting to the same thing.

notes.term: The deep places of poverty and famine
notes.note: “Although the fig tree shall not blossom, neither shall fruit be in the vines… yet I will rejoice in the LORD” ([[Hab.3.17-Hab.3.18|Habakkuk 3:17–18]]).
Before long.
The personal name of God in the Old Testament, printed “the LORD” in most English Bibles.
John Bunyan’s name in *The Pilgrim’s Progress* for the angels who welcome pilgrims into the Celestial City.
“Aijeleth Shahar,” the hind of the morning, is the tune named in the title of [[Ps.22.1|Psalm 22]], the psalm of the cross. Spurgeon makes it a name for Christ.
“Who shall ascend into the hill of the LORD?” ([[Ps.24.3|Psalm 24:3]]).

modern: A day is coming when the crown jewels of our great King will be counted, to see whether they match the inventory his Father gave him. My soul, will you be among the precious things of Jesus? You are precious to him if he is precious to you, and you will be his “in that day” if he is yours in this day.

In Malachi’s time, the Lord’s chosen ones used to talk with one another in such a way that their God himself listened to their talk. He liked it so much that he took notes of it—yes, and made a book of it, which he filed in his Record Office. Pleased with their conversation, he was pleased with them too. Stop, my soul, and ask yourself: if Jesus were to listen to your talk, would he be pleased with it? Is it to his glory, and does it build up the brothers and sisters? Speak, my soul, and be sure you tell the truth.

But what an honor it will be for us poor creatures to be counted by the Lord as his crown jewels! All the saints have this honor. Jesus not only says, “They are mine,” but, “They shall be mine.” He bought us, sought us, brought us in, and has so far shaped us into his image that he will fight for us with all his might.

notes.note: The Hebrew word means a special treasure: a king’s own prized possession.

notes.term: Answer to the inventory which His Father gave Him
notes.note: Jesus’ prayer: “Those that thou gavest me I have kept, and none of them is lost” ([[John.17.12|John 17:12]]).
“Then they that feared the LORD spake often one to another: and the LORD hearkened, and heard it, and a book of remembrance was written before him” ([[Mal.3.16|Malachi 3:16]]).
Building up in faith.
Counted; regarded.
Worked.

modern: What! Does God have power over the tongues of dogs? Can he keep mongrels from barking? Yes, he can. He can even stop an Egyptian dog from worrying one of the lambs of Israel’s flock. Does God silence dogs, and the doglike among men, and the great dog at hell’s gate? Then let’s go on our way without fear.

Even if he lets dogs move their tongues, he can still stop their teeth. They may make a dreadful noise and still do us no real harm. Yet how sweet quiet is! How delightful to move among enemies and see that God makes them be at peace with us! Like Daniel in the lions’ den, we are unhurt among destroyers.

Oh, that this word of the Lord to Israel might be true for me today! Is the dog worrying me? I’ll tell my Lord about him. Lord, he pays no attention to my pleading; you speak the word of power, and he must lie down. Give me peace, O my God, and let me see your hand in it so clearly that I may plainly see the difference your grace has made between me and the ungodly!

notes.note: Mongrel dogs, especially snappish ones.
Of a dog: biting and shaking another animal, harassing it.
People who snarl and snap like dogs. Paul warns, “Beware of dogs” ([[Phil.3.2|Philippians 3:2]]).

notes.term: The great dog at hell’s gate
notes.note: Satan, pictured as the watchdog at the gate of hell, like Cerberus in Greek myth.

notes.term: God maketh them to be at peace with us
notes.note: “When a man’s ways please the LORD, he maketh even his enemies to be at peace with him” ([[Prov.16.7|Proverbs 16:7]]).

notes.term: Daniel in the den of lions

modern: What’s recorded here is my own experience. I can set my seal to it that God is true. In very wonderful ways he has answered his servant’s prayers time after time. Yes, and he is hearing my present plea, and he isn’t turning his ear away from me. Blessed be his holy name!

What then? Why, the promise that lies sleeping in the psalmist’s believing confidence is surely mine too. Let me grasp it with the hand of faith: “The Lord will receive my prayer.” He will accept it, think about it, and grant it in the way and at the time his loving wisdom judges best. I bring my poor prayer in my hand to the great King, and he gives me an audience and graciously receives my request. My enemies won’t listen to me, but my Lord will. They ridicule my tearful prayers, but my Lord doesn’t; he takes my prayer into his ear and into his heart.

What a welcome this is for a poor sinner! We receive Jesus, and then the Lord receives us and our prayers for his Son’s sake. Blessed be that dear name which franks our prayers, so that they pass freely even through the golden gates. Lord, teach me to pray, since you hear my prayers.

notes.term: Set to my seal that God is true
notes.note: “He that hath received his testimony hath set to his seal that God is true” ([[John.3.33|John 3:33]]). To set your seal to something is to sign it as true.
A humble, earnest request; a prayer.
A formal hearing with a king.
A formal request.
To frank a letter was to mark it so it went through the post free. Christ’s name carries our prayers to God without charge.
The disciples’ request: “Lord, teach us to pray” ([[Luke.11.1|Luke 11:1]]).

modern: We believe in the eternal security of the saints. First, because they are Christ’s, and he will never lose the sheep he has bought with his blood and received from his Father.

Next, because he gives them eternal life, and if it is eternal, well then, it is eternal, and there can be no end to it—unless there can be an end to hell, and heaven, and God. If spiritual life can die out, it obviously isn’t eternal life but temporary life. But the Lord speaks of eternal life, and that firmly shuts out any possibility of an end.

Notice, further, that the Lord expressly says, “They shall never perish.” As long as words mean anything, this keeps believers from perishing. The most stubborn unbelief can’t force this meaning out of the sentence.

Then, to make the matter complete, he declares that his people are in his hand, and he defies all their enemies to snatch them out of it. Surely that’s impossible even for the fiend of hell. We must be safe in the grip of an Almighty Savior.
Let’s put away fleshly fear as well as fleshly confidence, and rest peacefully in the hollow of the Redeemer’s hand.

notes.term: The eternal security of the saints
notes.note: The teaching that those truly saved by Christ will never finally be lost. It is also called the perseverance of the saints.
“My Father, which gave them me, is greater than all” ([[John.10.29|John 10:29]]).
Effectively; in a way that actually does the job.
Snatch them away.
A devil.
Of the flesh: the desires of our fallen human nature, not only sexual ones.

modern: “If any of you lack wisdom.” There’s no “if” about it, for I am sure I lack it. What do I know? How can I find my own way? How can I direct others? Lord, I am a mass of foolishness, and I have no wisdom at all.

You say, “Let him ask of God.” Lord, I ask now. Here at your footstool I ask to be supplied with heavenly wisdom for today’s puzzles—yes, and for today’s simple things too, for I know I may do very stupid things even in plain matters unless you keep me out of mischief.

I thank you that all I have to do is ask. What grace this is on your part, that I have only to pray in faith and you will give me wisdom! Here you promise me a liberal education, and without an angry tutor or a scolding schoolmaster, too. And you will give it without a fee—give it to a fool who lacks wisdom. O Lord, I thank you for that definite and expressive word, “It shall be given him.” I believe it. Today you will make your little child know the hidden wisdom that the worldly wise never learn. You will guide me with your counsel, and afterward receive me to glory.

notes.note: Doesn’t scold or throw it back in your face.
Supplied, equipped.
Yes.
A play on words. A liberal education was a broad, gentleman’s schooling, and James says God gives “liberally,” that is, generously.
An assistant schoolmaster, often the strict one who kept order.

notes.term: The hidden wisdom which the carnally prudent never learn
notes.note: “Thou hast hid these things from the wise and prudent, and hast revealed them unto babes” ([[Matt.11.25|Matthew 11:25]]). The carnally prudent are those who are wise by worldly standards.

notes.term: Thou wilt guide me with thy counsel
notes.note: “Thou shalt guide me with thy counsel, and afterward receive me to glory” ([[Ps.73.24|Psalm 73:24]]).

modern: When true religion is ready to die out among the wealthy, it finds a home among the poor of this world, rich in faith. Even now the Lord has his faithful remnant. Am I one of them?

Perhaps it is because people are afflicted and poor that they learn to trust in the name of the Lord. Someone who has no money must see what he can do on trust. Someone whose own name is worth nothing in his own eyes does wisely to rest on another name, the best of all names, the name of Jehovah. God will always have a trusting people, and they will be an afflicted and poor people. Little as the world thinks of them, their being left in the middle of a nation is the channel of untold blessings to it. Here is the preserving salt that holds back the corruption that is in the world through lust.

Again the question comes home to each of us: Am I one of them? Am I afflicted by the sin within me and around me? Am I poor in spirit, poor spiritually in my own judgment? Do I trust in the Lord? That is the main thing. Jesus reveals the name, the character, the person of God; am I trusting in him? If so, I am left in this world for a purpose. Lord, help me to fulfill it.

notes.term: The poor of this world, rich in faith
notes.note: “Hath not God chosen the poor of this world rich in faith, and heirs of the kingdom?” ([[Jas.2.5|James 2:5]]).
The faithful few God keeps for himself when most fall away ([[Rom.11.5|Romans 11:5]]).
On credit: getting goods now and paying later, on the strength of someone’s good name. Spurgeon plays on the word.
The personal name of God in the Old Testament, printed “the LORD” in most English Bibles.
Preserving salt, which keeps food from going bad. “Ye are the salt of the earth” ([[Matt.5.13|Matthew 5:13]]).

notes.term: The corruption which is in the world through lust

notes.note: Any strong desire, especially a sinful one, not only sexual desire.
“Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” ([[Matt.5.3|Matthew 5:3]]).

modern: Yesterday we thought about the afflicted and poor people whom the Lord left to be a living seed in a dead world. The prophet says of them that they won’t do wrong or tell lies. So while they had neither rank nor riches to guard them, they also couldn’t use the weapons the wicked rely on so heavily: they could defend themselves neither by sin nor by cunning.

What then? Would they be destroyed? Not at all! They would both feed and rest, and be not only free from danger but even untroubled by the fear of harm. Sheep are very weak creatures, and wolves are terrible enemies; yet at this moment sheep outnumber wolves, and the cause of the sheep is always winning while the cause of the wolves is always losing ground. One day flocks of sheep will cover the plains, and not a wolf will be left. The fact is that sheep have a shepherd, and this gives them food, protection and peace. “None”—which means not one, whether in human or devilish form—“shall make them afraid.” Who will terrify the Lord’s flock when he is near? We lie down in green pastures, for Jesus himself is food and rest to our souls.

notes.term: They shall not work iniquity nor speak lies
notes.note: “The remnant of Israel shall not do iniquity, nor speak lies” ([[Zeph.3.13|Zephaniah 3:13]]). Iniquity means wickedness.
Cunning, craftiness.
Food, especially fodder for animals.
Devilish.
“He maketh me to lie down in green pastures” ([[Ps.23.2|Psalm 23:2]]).

modern: We won’t be ashamed of our faith. Nitpicking critics may attack the Scriptures we base our belief on, but every year the Lord will make it clearer that in his Book there is no error, no excess and no omission. It is no disgrace to be a simple believer. The faith that looks to Jesus alone is a crown of honor on anyone’s head, and better than a star on his chest.

We won’t be ashamed of our hope. It will be just as the Lord has said. We will be fed, led, blessed and given rest. Our Lord will come, and then the days of our mourning will be over. How we will glory in the Lord, who first gave us a living hope and then gave us what we hoped for!

We won’t be ashamed of our love. Jesus is altogether lovely to us, and never, never will we have to blush because we gave him our hearts. The sight of our glorious Well-beloved will justify the most passionate devotion to him. No one will blame the martyrs for dying for him. When the enemies of Christ are clothed with everlasting contempt, those who love Jesus will find themselves honored by all holy beings, because they chose the reproach of Christ rather than the treasures of Egypt.

notes.note: Nitpicking; always finding fault.
The star-shaped badge of a knighthood or other royal honor, worn on the chest.

notes.term: The days of our mourning shall be ended
notes.note: “And the days of thy mourning shall be ended” ([[Isa.60.20|Isaiah 60:20]]).
A living hope: “a lively hope by the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead” ([[1Pet.1.3|1 Peter 1:3]]).
“Yea, he is altogether lovely” ([[Song.5.16|Song of Solomon 5:16]]).
A name for Christ from the Song of Solomon: “A bundle of myrrh is my wellbeloved unto me” ([[Song.1.13|Song of Solomon 1:13]]).
“Some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt” ([[Dan.12.2|Daniel 12:2]]).

notes.term: The reproach of Christ rather than the treasures of Egypt
notes.note: Of Moses: “Esteeming the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures in Egypt” ([[Heb.11.26|Hebrews 11:26]]). Reproach means disgrace.

modern: The more we live apart, the safer we will be. God wants his people separate from sinners. His call to them is, “Come ye out from among them.” A Christian world is a monstrosity the Scriptures never imagine. A worldly Christian is spiritually diseased. Those who make compromises with Christ’s enemies may be counted among them.

Our safety doesn’t lie in coming to terms with the enemy, but in living alone with our best Friend. If we do this, we will live in safety despite the sarcasm, the slander and the sneers of the world. We will be safe from the deadly influence of its unbelief, its pride, its emptiness, its filth.
God will also make us live in safety alone in that day when sin is punished on the nations by wars and famines.

The Lord brought Abram from Ur of the Chaldeans, but he stopped halfway. He had no blessing until, having set out for the land of Canaan, into the land of Canaan he came. He was safe alone even surrounded by enemies. Lot wasn’t safe in Sodom, though he was in a circle of friends. Our safety is in living apart with God.

notes.note: In British English, any grain, not only maize.

notes.term: Come ye out from among them
notes.note: “Wherefore come out from among them, and be ye separate, saith the Lord” ([[2Cor.6.17|2 Corinthians 6:17]]).
Imagine; have in view.
Counted.
Harmful; deadly.
Emptiness, worthlessness: anything that promises much and gives nothing. Not only pride in your looks.

notes.term: Sin shall be visited on the nations
notes.note: To visit sin is to come and punish it.
Abram’s family set out from Ur for Canaan but settled in Haran on the way ([[Gen.11.31|Genesis 11:31]]). Later, “into the land of Canaan they came” ([[Gen.12.5|Genesis 12:5]]).

notes.term: Lot was not safe in Sodom
notes.note: Angels had to drag him out before the city was destroyed ([[Gen.19.15-Gen.19.16|Genesis 19:15–16]]).

modern: When the Lord himself speaks in his own person rather than through a prophet, the word carries a special weight for believing minds. It is Jehovah himself who keeps his own vineyard. He doesn’t trust it to anyone else, but makes it his own personal care. Aren’t they well kept whom God himself keeps?

We are to receive his gracious watering not only every day and every hour, “but every moment.” How we ought to grow! How fresh and fruitful every plant should be! What rich clusters the vines should bear!

But troublemakers come: little foxes, and the wild boar. So the Lord himself is our Guardian, and at all hours, both “night and day.” What, then, can harm us? Why are we afraid? He tends, he waters, he guards; what more do we need?

Twice in this verse the Lord says, “I will.” What truth, what power, what love, what unchangeableness we find in Jehovah’s great “I will”! Who can resist his will? If he says “I will,” what room is there for doubt? With an “I will” from God we can face all the armies of sin, death and hell. O Lord, since you say, “I will keep thee,” I answer, “I will praise thee!”

notes.note: Special, belonging particularly to someone (not odd).
The personal name of God in the Old Testament, printed “the LORD” in most English Bibles.
God’s people, pictured as his vineyard: “In that day sing ye unto her, A vineyard of red wine” ([[Isa.27.2|Isaiah 27:2]]; compare [[Isa.5.7|Isaiah 5:7]]).
“Take us the foxes, the little foxes, that spoil the vines” ([[Song.2.15|Song of Solomon 2:15]]).
“The boar out of the wood doth waste it” ([[Ps.80.13|Psalm 80:13]]), of the vine God brought out of Egypt.
Unchanging.
Armies.

modern: God’s choice of his people is the reason he stands by them and doesn’t forsake them. He chose them out of his love, and he loves them because of his choice. His own good pleasure is the source of their election, and his election is the reason his pleasure in them continues. It would dishonor his great name for him to forsake them, since it would show either that he made a mistake in his choice or that he was fickle in his love. God’s love has this glory, that it never changes, and he will never tarnish this glory.

By all our memories of the Lord’s past kindnesses, let’s rest assured that he won’t forsake us. He who has gone so far as to make us his people won’t undo the work of his grace. He hasn’t done such wonders for us only to leave us in the end. His Son Jesus has died for us, and we may be sure he hasn’t died in vain. Can he forsake those for whom he shed his blood? Because until now he has taken pleasure in choosing and saving us, it will still be his pleasure to bless us. Our Lord Jesus is no changeable Lover. Having loved his own, he loves them to the end.

notes.note: Standing by; staying loyal to.
God’s own free, glad decision: “according to the good pleasure of his will” ([[Eph.1.5|Ephesians 1:5]]).
God’s choice of his people for salvation.
Acts of loyal, unfailing love.
Worked.
Until now.

notes.term: Having loved His own, He loves them to the end
notes.note: “Having loved his own which were in the world, he loved them unto the end” ([[John.13.1|John 13:1]]).
